title: Mental Well-Being and the Influence of Place: Conceptual Approaches for the Built Environment for Planning Healthy and Walkable Cities
review_question: What elements of the built environment affect mental well-being according to international literature?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Keywords: “built environment”, “well-being”, “subjective well-being”, “mental well-being”. Database: Web of Science. Time frame: 1975-2020.

findings.antecedent: Urban green spaces
findings.quote: Urban green spaces have been shown to offer measurable benefits for health and mental well-being

findings.antecedent: Views of nature (residential or workplace windows)
findings.quote: seeing nature through residential or workplace windows can promote the reduction of stress and mental fatigue

findings.antecedent: Views of greenery
findings.quote: Views of greenery appear to also be beneficial for well-being.

findings.antecedent: View of greenery from hospital ward
findings.consequent: Recovery speed and need for pain relief
findings.quote: in hospitals, those with a view of greenery from their ward are more likely to get better quickly, with less need for pain relief

findings.antecedent: Experiencing nature (gardens, parks, flowers' scent, birdsong, water sounds)
findings.quote: sitting in gardens or parks, smelling the flowers' scent, listening to birds or hearing water can provide stress relief and greater positive emotions.

findings.antecedent: Vegetation and trees in urban spaces
findings.quote: Several studies find that vegetation and trees in urban spaces are associated with lower crime

findings.antecedent: Increased tree cover in urban areas
findings.consequent: Sense of safety and mental well-being benefits
findings.quote: increasing tree cover in urban areas may result in increased sense of safety with mental well-being benefits.

findings.antecedent: Being active in nature (fresh air, exercise)
findings.quote: being active in nature, fresh air and exercise are beneficial for mental well-being.

findings.antecedent: Proximity and access to parks and green spaces
findings.consequent: Opportunities for social interaction and physical activity
findings.quote: Proximity and access to parks and green spaces offer opportunities for social interaction

findings.antecedent: Private gardens
findings.consequent: Mental well-being (compensation for lack of public green spaces)
findings.quote: private gardens can also compensate for the lack of access to public green spaces, being a fundamental resource for mental well-being

findings.antecedent: Quality of green spaces
findings.quote: The 'quality' of green spaces is as important as 'quantity' and 'proximity'.

findings.antecedent: Walking
findings.quote: Walking is the most ancient form of urban transport, with important benefits for personal well-being and overall health

findings.antecedent: Greater neighborhood walkability
findings.quote: greater neighborhood walkability should generate an increase in walking

findings.antecedent: Active frontages (windows, retail, good quality lighting, street activity)
findings.consequent: Safety of streets and attractiveness for walkability
findings.quote: active frontages are important for safety of streets. Streets with windows, retail frontage, good quality lighting and street activity provide a much safer environment for pedestrians.

findings.antecedent: Shorter distances to a node of activity
findings.quote: various studies indicate that shorter distances to a node of activity can positively influence walking and mental well-being

findings.antecedent: Walkable communities
findings.consequent: Short-term mental well-being (cognitive/affective evaluations, happiness, satisfaction, relaxation, reduced anxiety/stress)
findings.quote: improvements in short-term mental well-being, demonstrated by cognitive and affective evaluations, raised levels of (hedonic) happiness, satisfaction, relaxation and reduced anxiety/stress

findings.antecedent: Highly walkable communities
findings.consequent: Interaction with environment, connection to community, responsibility, individual calm, community trust, perceived danger in public space
findings.quote: in highly walkable communities, residents can interact with their environment with more regularity and, therefore, feel more connected to and responsible for their community, increasing individual calm, community trust and decreasing perceived danger in public space

findings.antecedent: Wide sidewalks, active uses, trees on sidewalks
findings.quote: importance of wide sidewalks and active uses to ease walking, and also the importance of trees on sidewalks, which elicit wellbeing and happiness

findings.antecedent: Traffic noise, motorized traffic, narrow/deteriorated sidewalks, difficult crossings
findings.consequent: Walking (hindered) and stress (for children, women, older adults)
findings.quote: traffic noise, motorized traffic, narrow and deteriorated sidewalks and difficult crossings hinder walking, in particular for children, women and older adults, causing them stress

findings.antecedent: High-density locations (better access to services/workplaces, higher pedestrian traffic, greater interactions)
findings.quote: access to services and workplaces is better in high-density locations, where there is a higher proportion of pedestrian traffic and greater possibility for interactions and encounters between people, with benefits for mental well-being

findings.antecedent: High density urban areas (impersonal relations, weaker social relations, tall buildings on narrow streets)
findings.quote: urban areas with high density generate more impersonal and superficial relations between residents, making social relations weaker in high density urban areas, as well as in tall buildings on narrow streets, provoking stress and negatively affecting mental well-being

findings.antecedent: Higher density housing (restricted to terraced forms with front doors, roof terraces, grass verges, street trees)
findings.quote: higher density housing is restricted to terraced forms with front doors into the street and roof terraces, and street layouts which incorporate grass verges and street trees

findings.antecedent: Extreme density
findings.consequent: Residential satisfaction (negative), loss of privacy, noise exposure
findings.quote: extreme density tends to negatively affect residential satisfaction due to problems, including loss of privacy and exposure to noise

findings.antecedent: Streets with front gardens, paired and continuous housing (clear public/private space differentiation)
findings.quote: streets with front gardens provide more opportunities for interaction. Paired and continuous housing is suggested by various authors as positive for mental well-being, since it achieves a clear differentiation of public and private space

findings.antecedent: Low-density urban developments
findings.consequent: Calm, greater access to nature, strong interpersonal bonds
findings.quote: low-density urban developments can offer calm, greater access to nature and strong interpersonal bonds

findings.antecedent: Quality of urban forms
findings.consequent: Relaxation and reduced anxiety in public spaces
findings.quote: quality of urban forms affects the degree to which built environments promote relaxation and reduced anxiety in public spaces.

findings.antecedent: Smaller city blocks
findings.quote: Many studies have advocated for smaller city blocks due to their apparent benefits for walking

findings.antecedent: Blocks facing open spaces or façades with greater percentage of windows
findings.quote: Blocks which face open spaces or façades with a greater percentage of windows are also associated with greater mental well-being

findings.antecedent: High visibility of street façades (50-75%), accesses (doors) between 6-10 meters
findings.consequent: Active and safe streets, private/public space relationship, social opportunities, interaction with environment
findings.quote: High ranges of visibility of the street façades, from 50% to 75%, and accesses (doors) between six to ten meters are highly recommended to create active and safe streets. This allows greater opportunities for the relationship between the private and the public space, which increases social opportunities and the ability of people to interact with their environment

findings.antecedent: Variety of façades in smaller lengths
findings.consequent: Personality, diversity, positive eudaemonic emotions, satisfaction with environment
findings.quote: The variety of façades in smaller lengths would give personality and diversity to the street, generating more positive emotions of a eudaemonic type and satisfaction with the environment.

findings.antecedent: Very long or monotonous fronts (lacking windows, ornaments, accesses, blind walls, barren lots)
findings.consequent: Negative mental well-being, boredom, negative emotions, limited social opportunities, reduced interaction with environment
findings.quote: very long or monotonous fronts lacking characteristics including windows, ornaments or accesses for many meters, blind walls or barren lots may have negative effects on mental well-being which can create boredom and negative emotions, which also limit social opportunities and reduce the capacity for people to interact with their environment

findings.antecedent: Ratio of building height to street width
findings.quote: The ratio of building height to street width is also a key spatial design factor to promote mental well-being

findings.antecedent: Building heights excessively exceeding street width
findings.consequent: Feelings of claustrophobia and perceptions of insecurity
findings.quote: Building heights that excessively exceed the street width could lead to feelings of claustrophobia and perceptions of insecurity.

findings.antecedent: Correct building height/street width proportion
findings.consequent: Spatial comfort and positive benefits for mental well-being
findings.quote: A correct building height/street width proportion can generate greater spatial comfort and positive benefits for mental well-being

findings.antecedent: Building heritage / historical or artistic value
findings.consequent: Perceived well-being, happiness, positive mental well-being
findings.quote: building heritage is also associated with higher perceived well-being. Many studies consistently show that buildings with historical or artistic value could lead to feelings of happiness and positive mental well-being in streets and public spaces

findings.antecedent: Presence of trees in the street and wide sidewalks (3-4 meters wide, in good condition)
findings.quote: the presence of trees in the street and wide sidewalks (three or four meters wide), in good condition, are also associated with greater perceived well-being.

findings.antecedent: Built environments
findings.consequent: Social interaction in public spaces, residential satisfaction, eudaemonic happiness
findings.quote: Built environments have a major impact on promoting social interaction in public spaces, which positively impacts factors including residential satisfaction and eudaemonic happiness

findings.antecedent: Mixed uses (building level) and visual permeability (between lots and streets)
findings.consequent: Social interaction and perception of safety
findings.quote: importance of mixed uses at the building level and visual permeability between lots and streets to contribute to social interaction and the perception of safety.

findings.antecedent: Spaces with high mixed uses
findings.consequent: Perceived social support and angst levels
findings.quote: spaces with high mixed uses are related to greater level of perceived social support and lower angst levels

findings.antecedent: Mix of uses (shops, pubs)
findings.quote: A mix of uses can encourage social interaction as people meet at local facilities such as shops and pubs.

findings.antecedent: Certain uses (industrial, late-night bars)
findings.quote: certain uses such as industrial ones or late-night bars may cause stress through noise irritation.

findings.antecedent: Many commercial properties in a residential area (shut at night)
findings.quote: having many commercial properties in a residential area can cause concern for safety when they are shut up at night

findings.antecedent: Greater density
findings.quote: greater density is also often associated with increased urban vitality

findings.antecedent: Hyper density (extreme vitality)
findings.quote: Extreme vitality caused by extreme density in urban areas may generate stress and negatively affect mental health

findings.antecedent: Homes on streets with more intense vehicular traffic and noise
findings.quote: people in homes on streets with more intense vehicular interact less with their neighbors than those in less congested streets

findings.antecedent: Chronic noise exposure (high congestion, crowds)
findings.consequent: Mental well-being, satisfaction with life, stress, angst, perceived spatial safety
findings.quote: chronic noise exposure, like in an intersection between avenues with high congestion or crowds of people, can affect mental well-being, generating problems which can reduce satisfaction with life, increase stress and angst and reduce perceived spatial safety

findings.antecedent: Noise from traffic, airplanes, trains, industrial processes, construction work, noisy neighbors
findings.quote: Traffic is the source of most noise in urban zones, but other sources can also cause problems: noise from airplanes, trains, industrial processes, construction work or noisy neighbors.

findings.antecedent: Acceptable sound insulation in buildings (external and internal noise)
findings.quote: acceptable sound insulation in buildings, both from external and internal noise, is essential.

findings.antecedent: Trees and other forms of greenery
findings.quote: trees and other forms of greenery can also mitigate the effect of noise annoyance

findings.antecedent: Soundscape
findings.quote: the “soundscape” can act positively to increase mental well-being in environments.

findings.antecedent: Birdsong, sound of water or wetlands
findings.quote: birdsong, the sound of water or wetlands, tend to relax tensions and increase positive emotions in environments.

findings.antecedent: Maintenance and enhancement of local flora and fauna in urban parks and green open spaces
findings.quote: maintenance and enhancement of local flora and fauna in urban parks and green open spaces help promote positive emotions for mental well-being

findings.antecedent: Urban squares (for people to relax, communicate, see others and be seen), soundscape identity
findings.quote: importance of urban squares for people to relax, to communicate, to see others and to be seen, in which soundscape identity is important for a designated space

findings.antecedent: Natural sounds in urban squares
findings.quote: natural sounds as a group are generally preferred in urban squares, with differences between age groups.

findings.antecedent: Older people (sounds relating to nature, culture, human activities)
findings.quote: Older people are more favorable to sounds relating to nature, culture, or human activities.

findings.antecedent: Younger people (music and mechanical sounds)
findings.quote: younger people are more favorable to music and mechanical sounds

synthesis_conclusions: Studies on built environments and mental well-being are recent, with a significant increase in publications since 2012.

Scientific production is concentrated in developed countries (England, USA, Australia, Scotland, Canada, Germany, New Zealand, China), with a notable lack of studies in the Global South, particularly Latin America.

Research is predominantly quantitative (standardized surveys, regressive models, indicators), with qualitative approaches being scarcer, especially for social interaction, spatial design, and walkability.
Urban planning and design can either promote or disincentivize elements of the built environment that positively impact mental well-being.
In Chile, urban planning instruments lack explicit reference to mental well-being or subjective well-being.

While no single 'formula' exists, environmental design can foster positive emotional bonds by creating attractive public spaces with natural elements, promoting social interaction, and inviting walking and relaxation, leading to more walkable and sustainable environments.

There is a critical need for more research in Latin America on how the built environment affects mental health, contributing empirical results to public policies, and understanding positive/negative elements from diverse community experiences (age, gender, socio-cultural differences).
evidence_gaps: Lack of studies on built environments and mental well-being in the Global South, especially Latin America.
Scarcity of qualitative studies, particularly for social interaction, spatial design, and walkability.
Underrepresentation of studies from social sciences (Geography, Urbanism, Architecture) compared to environmental sciences (Public Environmental and Occupational Health).
Absence of explicit mental well-being concepts in Chilean urban planning instruments.
Need for empirical results from urbanism to inform public policies in Latin America.
Need to understand differential impacts of built environment elements on mental well-being across age, gender, and socio-cultural differences.
limitations: Most evidence comes from quantitative methods (standardized surveys, regressive models, indicators), with qualitative approximations being scarcer.
The review primarily used the Web of Science database; other platforms (Scopus, PubMed) could complement findings and reveal additional data sources, especially from the Global South.

paper_metadata.title: Mental Well-Being and the Influence of Place: Conceptual Approaches for the Built Environment for Planning Healthy and Walkable Cities
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Mental Well-Being and the Influence of Place: Conceptual Approaches for the Built Environment for Planning Healthy and Walkable Cities
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Promotion of healthy cities has prompted urban planners and designers to build new conceptual frameworks to improve the design of public spaces, in which mental well-being emerges as a fundamental concept. Mental well-being is related to spatial design, with increasing attention being paid to the built environment as an important predictor of mental well-being. The objective of this article is to advance and contribute new knowledge about the characteristics of the built environment and its potential benefits for mental well-being. A meta-analysis is carried out on various empirical and theoretical approaches from the literature. Using a WOS database as a case study, a methodology based on a bibliometric analysis is proposed to examine which elements of the built environment impact mental well-being in research between 1975 and 2020, using the HistCites and VOSviewer tools. The results show that there are six thematic axes related to the built environment that would favor greater mental well-being in public spaces: walkability, density, spatial design, environmental noise, green areas and social interaction. The six thematic axes are critically analyzed and integrated into a conceptual framework to address the impacts of the built environment on mental well-being in the planning of cities. It concludes with a discussion on the implications of these concepts for urban public policy and the promotion of healthier and more sustainable and walkable environments in Latin American cities.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Exposure to natural elements in urban green spaces can restore directed attention and reduce mental fatigue, contributing to mental well-being.
Contact with natural environments in cities can lead to physiological stress reduction and positive emotional states, enhancing mental well-being.
The built environment can be designed to enhance individuals' sense of coherence and provide generalized resistance resources, promoting health and well-being.
Mental well-being is influenced by multiple interacting levels of the built environment, from individual perceptions to public policies, which should be considered in urban planning.

mechanism_chain.description: Pathways through which urban green spaces influence mental well-being, primarily via psychological restoration and opportunities for health-promoting behaviors.
